Biggest movers of the last 12 months, and why

By sector

Last four weeks · Oct 23 to Nov 20, 2026 · prices refreshed Nov 20

The AI trade unwound, and took the index with it. Most stocks barely moved.

In 30 seconds
  • What happened: the S&P 500 fell 9.4% in four weeks and 11.6% from its Oct 6 record, into a correction. The typical stock fell only 2.5%, and the equal-weight index 4.2%: the damage was concentrated in AI chips (−25%), AI hardware (−23%), crypto stocks (−23%) and software (−16%).
  • Why: a crowded AI trade met three blows at once: Nvidia's CEO resigned after a personal scandal and an SEC probe was reported; strong earnings stopped protecting expensive stocks (ServiceNow −27% in a day, Datadog −14% despite beating); and the Fed turned hawkish, with a half-point December hike floated.
  • What held up: consumer staples (+3%) and utilities (+2%) rose. Oil fell 19% as the US held off strikes on Iran and Hormuz traffic recovered; bitcoin fell 26% and even gold fell 12%, a sign of investors raising cash wherever they could.
  • What to do: stay invested, rebalance, harvest tax losses before Dec 31, and don't rush back into AI chips until the selling stops. The plan by horizon is below.

How to position: the next 1, 3, 6 and 12 months

Read with the early-warning signals on the CEO memo and the Downturn Ledger's plan by stage. General education, not personal advice: fit it to your own timeline and taxes.

1 monthto late December

Fear is high (VIX 36) and the selling is forced. Next: PCE inflation Nov 25, jobs Dec 4, Fed Dec 8–9.

Do
Stay invested. Rebalance to your target mix, which after this drop means adding a little to stocks. Sell losers before Dec 31 to bank tax losses, buying a similar (not identical) fund to stay invested. If you have new cash, invest it in thirds: now, at S&P 6,600 (−15%) and at 6,255 (−20%).
Avoid
Selling after a 10% fall; buying back AI chips because they look cheap while they are still falling.
Change course if
The S&P 500 closes below 6,255, a bear market: switch to the Downturn Ledger's bear-market steps.
3 monthsto February

The Fed decision, Big Tech's 2027 spending budgets in late-January earnings, and the Medicare audit rule (comments close Jan 19) set the next leg.

Do
Keep the 5–10% tilt in businesses whose profits don't depend on AI spending: banks, staples, beaten-down software (in stages). Hold health insurers until the audit rule is clearer. Keep bonds short-dated while the Fed is hiking.
Avoid
Long-dated bonds while rates may rise; any single stock above 5% of the portfolio.
Change course if
Big Tech holds its budgets and AI hardware climbs back above its 200-day average: add chips and hardware in stages. Budgets cut: trim them further, add to staples and health care.
6 monthsto May

Too far to forecast, close enough to plan. Decide now which signpost triggers which shift.

Soft landing
Oil stays under $85, inflation cools, the Fed stops. Like 2023 and 2025: the dip recovers, and the broad market and equal-weight lead.
AI unwind
Capex budgets cut. Like 2000–02: staples, health care, value and quality bonds held up.
Inflation sticks
Core inflation 0.3%+ a month, more hikes. Like 2022: T-bills and energy; stocks and bonds both fall.
Credit break
Junk-bond spreads above 5%, unemployment up half a point. Like 2008 and 2020: long Treasuries, gold, cash.
12 monthsto November 2027

Lower prices raise the expected return if profits hold up. Corrections without a recession (2023, 2025) recovered within months; recessions (2001, 2008) took years.

Do
Hold your target mix: about 70% total-market index, 15% equal-weight, 15% international. Rebalance in January and re-score the add and cut lists after January earnings.
Avoid
Waiting for the bottom to buy: the best days came right after the worst ones in 2025.
Change course if
Recession signals hit (unemployment up half a point from its low, junk spreads above 5%): hold 2–3 years of planned spending in T-bills, but keep the stock core.

What the month did to our calls

Since the add and cut lists were set on Nov 6, the add list's middle stock fell 7.7%, the cut list's 5.8%, the S&P 500 6.3% and the typical stock 3.6%. Two weeks is too short to judge, but the pattern is clear: the cyclical adds (Cummins, Expedia, Steel Dynamics) fell on growth worries.

The theme calls did better: the two cuts fell hardest (crypto −23%, Magnificent Seven −12%) and AI chips, held back until the selling stopped, fell 25%.

One change: health insurers move from Add to Hold. On Nov 16 Medicare proposed wider audits that could claw back about $9 billion a year from insurers; UnitedHealth fell 14% in a week. Revisit after comments close on Jan 19 and insurers give 2027 guidance.

One to watch: oil's 19% fall weakens the case for oil stocks (Hold) and helps airlines and consumers, which were set aside as a bet on oil.

What the month taught

  • Crowded trades fall together and fast. AI chips lost a quarter of their value in four weeks while the typical stock lost 2.5%.
  • The index is not the market. The S&P 500's 9% fall came mostly from a few giants; 38% of stocks rose.
  • Good results don't protect an expensive stock. ServiceNow raised its AI target and fell 27% in a day; Datadog beat forecasts and fell 14%.
  • Key-person risk is real. The world's most valuable chipmaker lost 40% in a month after its founder left.
  • In a rush for cash, everything sells. Gold and bitcoin fell alongside stocks; only short-term Treasuries and staples held.

Sources: Yahoo Finance prices to Nov 20, 2026; The Closing Print and Journal Arta (Nov 20); Trefis on ServiceNow (Nov 18); The Motley Fool on Marvell (Nov 16) and Datadog (Nov 4); TIKR on UnitedHealth and Chipotle; Gulf News on oil (Nov 11); Trefis and Stocktwits on AppLovin.

CEO brief · one page

Own the market, but stop letting a few AI giants be the bet

Since 2023 the index beat 70% of its own stocks, carried by AI. Now the AI trade is unwinding: by Nov 20 the S&P 500 was 11.6% below its Oct 6 record, its 2026 gain down to about 1%, with Nvidia off 23% in a week. Corrections like this came in 2023 and 2025 and were recovered within months. Don't sell into it: keep a 90% index core and use the drop to tilt 5–10% toward growers priced below their sector.

Why it happened: six forces behind 2023–2026 Durable

ForceHow it played outThe durable truth
1 · The AI build-out moved down the supply chainThe spenders led first, then their suppliers, then the suppliers' bottlenecks. Magnificent Seven +109% → +62% → +25% → +9% (2023→26); power for AI +104% in 2024; AI hardware (memory, optics, servers) +105% in 2025 and +83% in 2026.In a building boom, profit flows to whoever owns the scarcest input and moves on as each bottleneck is solved. The spender pays first and is judged last.
2 · AI started eating incumbentsSoftware +55% → +12% → −15% → −12%. Stocks whose fall was blamed on AI: 1 in 2024, 20 in 2025, 70 in 2026 (AppLovin, Fair Isaac, Gartner, Reddit).Markets price a threat years before it shows in revenue. A moat is only as wide as the cost of copying it.
3 · Money stopped being freeThe 10-year Treasury yield stayed around 4–5% all four years (about 5% in November), against 2–3% through the 2010s. Homebuilders +53% in 2023, then −5% in 2025; real estate −5% in 2025.Interest rates are gravity: they set what future profits are worth today. Long-dated assets (housing, real estate, unprofitable growth) feel it first.
4 · Shocks vs. regime changesTariffs hit 158 stocks in 2025 and the index fell 19%, then recovered within months. The Iran war lifted energy's middle stock 37% and oil stocks 54% in 2026; defense rose 43% in 2025.Buy shocks, respect regimes. A one-time scare reverses; a lasting change in who pays what (rearmament, a closed shipping lane) reprices for years.
5 · Abnormal demand normalizes, with a lagCOVID winners collapsed in 2023 (Moderna −45%, Pfizer −41%). Health insurers fell 21% in 2024 as post-COVID care costs surged, then rose 38% in 2026 once prices were reset.Extreme profits and losses both revert. Businesses that reprice once a year (insurers) recover one to two years after costs spike.
6 · The consumer split in twoConsumer-discretionary middle stock +23% → +1% (2023→26). Firms hurt by weak shoppers fell every year: Dollar General, Lululemon, Nike, Deckers.Averages hide splits. Households with assets (stocks doubled) kept spending; lower-income shoppers squeezed by prices and rates traded down.

Investing rules that held every year: own the index (only 30% of stocks beat it) · judge a return against the spread, not against zero · don't chase (36% of 2024's top fifth repeated in 2025) · stay in (2025's +17.9% was −2.5% without its five best days).

What to add, what to cut

Every stock gets an outlook score from 0 to 100, built mostly from business fundamentals: how fast earnings are expected to grow, whether forecasts are rising, and what you pay for that growth against its sector. Price trend counts for only a tenth. Each also gets an expected 12-month return. Groups first, because a fund is the simplest way to act; then single stocks.

By group

Middle score and average expected return of each group's stocks. Example funds track each group; check holdings and costs before buying.

By stock

The 12 highest and lowest scores, at most two per sector. Add ideas need an expected return above 10%; stocks up more than 100% in a year are left off, since their earnings may be at a cyclical peak. Every candidate was then checked by hand against current news: stocks whose numbers are distorted by deals, one-off charges or the wrong comparison, or whose case rests on a commodity call such as oil, are set aside and listed with the reason. Click a ticker to mark it across the dashboard.

How the outlook score works, and how it would have done

25% · Earnings growth

Growth analysts expect over the next year (today's P/E on past earnings ÷ P/E on forecast earnings), plus revenue growth against a year ago.

15% · Forecast changes

How much next year's earnings forecast has moved over about three months. Rising forecasts tend to keep rising.

25% · Price against value

Price ÷ forecast earnings against the sector's middle stock, and against its own growth rate (the PEG ratio). Cheaper scores higher.

15% · Cash

Free cash flow and dividends as a share of the stock's market value.

10% · Main force

The force most often named for the stock in 2025–26 (AI spending, rates…), scored by how stocks it pushed did the next year.

10% · Price trend

Only as a check: a stock in a downtrend loses a little, since the market may know something the forecasts don't yet.

Expected 12-month return = dividend yield + 35% of expected earnings growth (capped at 60%) + 15% of the gap between the stock's P/E and its sector's, then shifted so the S&P 500 as a whole expects about 7%, near its long-run average. Analyst forecasts run optimistic, so only part of the growth is counted. The likely range is the middle half of outcomes given how much the stock has swung over the past year. Data: Yahoo Finance as of Nov 6, 2026.

Watch lists

Stocks that pass simple, stated rules on today's prices, at most two per sector. Each comes with why it qualifies, the price that would prove it wrong, and the force to watch. These are candidates to research, not instructions to trade.

What changed since October 9

Oct 5

The 10-year Treasury yield closed at 5.31%, its highest since 2002, on inflation worries. It eased to about 4.93% by Oct 30.

Oct 6

The S&P 500 set its latest record high.

October

Oil rose about 15% and Brent neared $118 a barrel on Strait of Hormuz shipping disruptions. Headline inflation rose to 3.7%.

Oct 28

The Fed held rates at 3.75–4.00% in a 10–2 vote; both dissenters wanted another hike.

Oct 29–30

Big Tech results showed AI spending outrunning cash flow: Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon and Meta spent $201.9 billion on property and equipment in the quarter against $175.5 billion of operating cash flow. Alphabet fell 12.6%, its worst day since listing.

Oct 30

Intel fell 28.6% on a weak outlook and pulled chip stocks down: the semiconductor index fell 7.2% that day. In October the Nasdaq fell 5.3% while the equal-weight S&P 500 rose 5.0%.

Nov 3

Midterm elections: Democrats won control of the House and Senate from January, so Washington will be divided.

Nov 4

Stocks rallied: the S&P 500 rose 1.6% as oil fell more than 8% and yields eased, with consumer stocks leading.

Sources: Suttle Crossland, November outlook; Portfolio Terminal, week of Oct 30; Defiant Capital, October update; Fidelity, midterms and stocks. Index moves and everything else on this page are from the price data.

How to monitor it

Recheck these once a week. The right-hand column says what would change the picture.

Rules behind the watch lists. Joining the rotation: in a downtrend on Oct 9, now back above its 200-day average by up to 8%, and no named force pushing it down. Pullback in a leader: above its 200-day average, ahead of the index over 6 months, 7–25% below its 52-week high after a down month, and no force pushing it down. Broken leader: leading or in an uptrend on Oct 9, now below both its 50- and 200-day averages. Stuck in a downtrend: below both averages then and now, more than 15 points behind the index over 6 months, with its main force pushing down. Stretched: 60% or more above its 200-day average after a 40%+ three months. Rules like these follow trends; they are wrong whenever a trend reverses sharply, as AI hardware just did.

Does company age matter?

Stocks grouped by how long they had been listed, or how long ago the company was founded, at the start of 2023.

Age measured from
Period

Treat the young-company result with care. Young companies in today's index mostly got in by soaring first (Palantir joined in 2024, AppLovin and Robinhood in 2025, each after a big run), while companies that listed and then faded never made it in. Across all US listings, long-running studies of IPOs, notably by Jay Ritter at the University of Florida, find that newly listed companies have on average trailed comparable established companies over their first few years. Listing dates come from Yahoo Finance, whose records start in 1962, and spin-offs count from their own listing.

The smallest fifth looks strong for the same reason young companies do: many small companies on today's list were added to the index after their shares soared, while small companies that slumped dropped out. Over longer histories, small companies have sometimes led and sometimes lagged.

Into 2027: forces to watch

The forces most often named for 2026 so far, what happened the following year to stocks they lifted or hit in the past, and the signs that would push their stocks up or down next year. These are signposts to watch, not predictions.

How these were calculated

Each annual figure is the change from the last trading day of the prior year to the last trading day of that year. With dividends uses dividend-adjusted closing prices (total return). Price only uses closing prices adjusted for splits and spin-offs. 2026 runs from December 31, 2025 to the as-of date above. The Since 2023 column compounds every year through the as-of date. Trend now uses daily closes with dividends: the 50- and 200-day averages, the return over the last 63 trading days, the gap from the 52-week high, and the 6-month return against the S&P 500. The line chart uses the last close of each week.

The one-sentence explanations were written by Claude, guided by each stock's largest one-day moves. Those for 2023 to 2025 draw mainly on its knowledge of widely reported events. Those for 2026 rest on news headlines where it could read them and are the least verified: where no cause could be confirmed, the sentence describes the move in general terms. None is individually sourced, so check one before relying on it.

The list is the index's membership today, not its membership in each year. Companies removed from the index since 2023 are absent, and some stocks shown joined partway through.

Trends and Lessons use the same prices. Trend lines and industry cells are simple averages across the stocks in each group. Deepest falls and best-day figures use daily closes with dividends. Index contributions are approximate, as noted beside that chart. Random portfolios hold equal amounts of each stock for the whole period with no trading.

Drivers: Claude tagged each one-sentence explanation with up to three forces from a fixed list of 19, each marked as pushing that stock up or down. The tags inherit any errors in the sentences, and counts show how often a force was named, not how much of the move it caused. "What came next" compares each stock's return in the following period with the average stock's, pooled over 2023 to 2026 so far.

Lessons on age, size and dividends: listing dates are Yahoo Finance's first trading dates; founding years come from the constituents list; sizes are rebuilt from share counts at the end of 2022. Groups compare the typical (middle) stock, so a few huge winners do not dominate.

Big picture: yearly pace is the compound annual return since the end of 2022; swings are the standard deviation of weekly returns, scaled to a year. The projection runs 2,000 simulated paths month by month using the growth rate and swings you choose. The long-run setting uses about 10% a year, roughly the S&P 500's compound return since 1926 (its simple average is a little over 12%, per Dimensional).

Three years is one stretch of market history, led by a small group of very large technology companies. Patterns that held here may not hold in a different one, and nothing on this page predicts the return of any single stock.
